title: Consistency describes agreement
summary: Compare fresh and delayed reads across copies. Use a book checkout to explain consistency promises and the choices made during a network break.
introduction: Two desks may hold different copies of the same book list. If one desk updates its list first, the other desk may briefly show an old answer. A consistency rule tells us what readers are allowed to see.
learningObjectives: Describe a strong-read promise and eventual consistency
Match a consistency choice to a library action
Explain the tradeoff during a network partition

blocks.text: A consistency rule describes how reads relate to writes. For this lesson, a **strong** rule means that after a write succeeds, a later read of that item sees that write or a newer one. Readers should not go back to an older saved value.
With **eventual consistency**, copies should agree after updates stop and communication and repair can finish. The term alone does not promise a fixed number of seconds before agreement.

A **network partition** is a communication break between parts of a system. Two desks can both be running while their link is broken. Neither can safely assume that the other desk has made no changes.

items: There is one physical copy of a book. Desk A records a successful checkout.
Desk B's replica still says available because it has not received the change.
An eventual read may show available. A later successful strong read must respect the completed checkout.
The checkout action itself also needs an atomic rule that checks and reserves the copy together. Fresh reads alone do not stop two simultaneous writers.

blocks.code:
ONE BOOK COPY, TWO DESKS
Start: A and B both show "available".
A saves checkout and confirms success.
B has not received that change yet.

Eventual read at B: may still show "available".
Strong read after success: must show the checkout or a newer state.

DURING A BROKEN LINK
Option 1: delay or refuse work that cannot keep the strong promise.
Option 2: let separated parts answer, allowing old/conflicting states.
Choose a rule for each action, and plan how conflicts are resolved.
blocks.title: Consistency describes agreement plan

blocks.text: For a book description, a slightly old sentence may be acceptable. For lending the last physical copy, the design needs a safe check-and-update rule and may need to refuse a request when it cannot be certain.

One rule is called the **CAP theorem**. It applies when parts of a system cannot talk. The system cannot promise both one agreed order for reads and writes and a successful answer to every request at every working part. To keep the first promise, some requests may have to wait or fail.

rows: A recent edit may take time to appear
Can keep the rule about one active loan per copy
Some requests may wait or fail during communication trouble
Helps a user see their own recent change
This is a narrower promise than making every reader immediately agree

blocks.text: Even when the network works, stronger coordination can add travel and waiting. Measure that cost against the actual correctness need instead of choosing one policy for every fact.

If two disconnected sides both accept edits, a later merge needs clear rules. Last-write-wins may discard an edit and depends on ordering rules; it is not automatically correct for payments, bookings, or loans.

items: Choose a consistency policy for a public book description and for lending the last copy. Explain one cost for each.
A description may allow delayed reads. Lending needs an atomic authoritative decision, which may reject work during a partition rather than promise the same copy twice.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not say eventual means immediate, or that CAP simply means pick any two. Name the exact read/write promise and what happens when communication breaks.
